title: When Does Dynamics Randomization Test Context Inference?

paper.title: When Does Dynamics Randomization Test Context Inference?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Environments with randomized dynamics are widely used to ask whether world
models need explicit context inference. However, randomization can leave
little predictive information for a context encoder to add, because distinct
latent parameters may produce similar transitions at visited states, or those
states may already reveal the active context. We formalize the remaining
one-step information as predictive headroom and compare kernels under
fixed and visited state–action distributions to distinguish changes in query
coverage from changes in context weights. We analyze discrete and continuous
environments and find low headroom both when kernels differ little and when
visitation reduces an otherwise large discrepancy. At the same time, resetting
state components increases headroom, showing that context evidence accumulates
in state. We propose reporting this headroom alongside the randomized
parameters, so that gains from explicit context inference can be interpreted
relative to the information missing from the current state and action.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In model-based RL, environments with randomized dynamics are commonly used to test whether world models benefit from explicit context inference. Latent physical parameters, such as masses and forces, can vary across episodes, and models that infer the active context are compared against context-blind predictors. However, a benchmark can randomize parameters and still leave a context mechanism little predictive information to add. Contextual MDPs formalize latent dynamics that vary across episodes [ 4 , 2 ] . Online system identification conditions a policy on parameters inferred from recent experience [ 7 ] . Adaptive dynamics models [ 6 ] and context-aware predictors [ 5 , 3 ] use experience to improve prediction under changing parameters. While those methods make predictive structure explicit, we quantify how much information about transitions the current state withholds before any such mechanism is added. We identify two mechanisms that can reduce the remaining predictive information. First, kernels that differ substantially across the state space may differ little at the visited state–action pairs. A wall, for example, can block the displacement induced by wind. Second, the dynamics can make visited states already informative about the hidden parameter. For instance, a persistent force changes both position and velocity, so the current state can contain information accumulated over earlier transitions. Even a memoryless model can then use this evidence without a history encoder. A small gain from revealing the true context can thus reflect weak kernel differences or implicit identification. We introduce an experimental diagnostic of context information under a given visitation. We compare transition kernels under a fixed reference and at visited state–action pairs using prior context weights, then reweight contexts by visitation to estimate the remaining predictive headroom. We show, in discrete and continuous settings, that similar headroom can arise from differing kernel variation. We propose reporting this measure when comparing world models, because explicit context inference can add predictive information only where the inputs miss it.

sections.heading: 3 Controlled evidence
sections.text: Environments. MiniGrid [ 1 ] provides an enumerable state space ( x , y , d ) (x,y,d) , with position and direction on an Empty-8x8 grid. We use a Wind variation that samples independent drift coordinates from 𝒰 ⁡ [ − v max , v max ] \mathcal{U}[-v_{\max},v_{\max}] . After each native action, each axis moves one cell in the sampled direction with probability equal to its drift magnitude, subject to wall blocking. In another variation, Resistance samples an action-failure probability ϵ ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , ϵ max ] \epsilon\sim\mathcal{U}[0,\epsilon_{\max}] , and a failed action leaves the state unchanged. Finally, we consider Point-Mass-Attractor as a continuous two-dimensional system with observed position and velocity, where one of four hidden corners ( ± 1.5 , ± 1.5 ) (\pm 1.5,\pm 1.5) exerts force − k ⁡ ( 𝐩 − θ ) -k(\mathbf{p}-\theta) alongside the action, with independent position and velocity noise and reflecting boundaries. We experiment with 5,000 5{,}000 episodes in each setting under uniform random actions: up to 256 256 steps in MiniGrid and 50 50 in Attractor, where the fixed episode length avoids duration-induced context reweighting. Context labels are logged for the diagnostic and excluded from the state–action predictive information set. We evaluate transition prediction without training policies or comparing returns. Estimation. MiniGrid’s structural reference is uniform over interior positions, four directions, and seven actions. There, we enumerate the kernels and integrate the continuous context prior. Visited headroom averages exact kernel KL divergences against mixtures fitted at each ( s , a ) (s,a) pair, leaving out the scored episode and applying one pseudo-count of smoothing. In Attractor, we use its query-invariant interior Gaussian kernel for the prior references. Its visited estimate scores logged next states under the known kernels, including boundary reflection, against a mixture with a five-fold, episode-split nearest-neighbor context posterior. The estimates retain all transitions. MiniGrid refits its mixtures, whereas Attractor resamples fixed per-episode contributions. Attractor neighbor-count selection uses the scored folds’ context labels, and its intervals omit posterior refitting uncertainty. We report fitted-predictor estimates, rather than exact mutual information, along with uncertainties. Implementation details are deferred to Appendix A . Attractor’s structural curve uses the interior Gaussian reference. Shading shows bootstrap intervals. Table 1: Comparisons at representative settings. Fixed and matched columns retain prior context weights, while visited headroom uses fitted visitation-dependent weights. Attractor’s identical prior references use its query-invariant interior kernel. Uncertainties are the larger one-sided deviations from the 95 % 95\% bootstrap intervals. Figure 1 illustrates that visited headroom can remain low as dynamics variation increases. In Wind (Table 1 ), matching the query distribution reduces the reference by 29 % 29\% , so coverage accounts for part of the difference. Using visitation-dependent context weights at those same queries removes a further 88 % 88\% of the matched reference. This comparison measures changes in context weights under the collection distribution, including any shift in marginal context frequencies. In Resistance, prior-weighted separation changes little under either comparison, and visited headroom retains about 93 % 93\% of the matched reference. Its low headroom mostly reflects weak kernel differences under these query and action weights. In Attractor, the prior reference is large but estimated visited headroom is about 11 % 11\% of that interior reference. Reset Wind Attractor None 0.078 ± 0.002 0.078\pm 0.002 0.112 ± 0.002 0.112\pm 0.002 Full, every 10 steps 0.411 ± 0.006 0.411\pm 0.006 ( + 430 % ) (+430\%) 0.473 ± 0.004 0.473\pm 0.004 ( + 324 % ) (+324\%) Full, every 2 steps 0.723 ± 0.017 0.723\pm 0.017 ( + 833 % ) (+833\%) — Position only, every 10 steps — 0.143 ± 0.003 0.143\pm 0.003 ( + 28 % ) (+28\%) State-component resets. We reset selected components before recording the current state, keeping the episode context and uniform action rule unchanged. Wind resamples valid position and direction uniformly, while Attractor resamples position uniformly in [ − 2 , 2 ] 2 [-2,2]^{2} and either zeroes or preserves velocity. Table 2 shows that frequent Wind resets increase predictive headroom. In Attractor, resetting both position and velocity raises headroom more than resetting position alone. The resets leave the transition family fixed while changing both query coverage and the posterior over context. The baseline Wind comparison separates these contributions, but no reset-specific matched references are reported. The reset comparisons show that context information accumulates in state, including velocity, but do not isolate its effect from changes in coverage.

sections.heading: 4 Implications for evaluating world models
sections.text: Low headroom can explain a small gain from explicit context inference when the observed state already supplies most of the evidence needed for prediction. High headroom instead indicates that revealing context can improve prediction. However, one should separately measure which information a learned representation retains and how well its predictor uses it, since a context encoder can still improve learning or approximation even when headroom is low. Comparisons of predictors with and without explicit context inference should therefore measure both the information available in the inputs and the errors of the actual models under matched data and compute. We propose reporting whether a benchmark’s context-conditional kernels remain predictively distinct at overlapping observed states. This requires specifying the collection rule, predictive inputs, transition weighting, and marginal context frequencies d ⁡ ( θ ) d(\theta) relative to the design prior. A low matched reference suggests changing the queries or perturbations, whereas a large matched-to-visited reduction requires distinguishing context imbalance from information retained in state. Increasing the parameter range alone does not resolve either issue reliably. We can compute these comparisons from context labels and simulator kernels, but with learned kernels we must also account for prediction error. Initial-state distributions, episode length, and observed physical coordinates also influence how much context remains hidden. A reset that changes position but preserves velocity can retain context information that the benchmark is intended to withhold. We therefore recommend reporting matched-query variation under each reset protocol’s collection distribution to separate changes in the prediction support from changes in context weights when interpreting the resulting headroom. We note that our measurements concern one-step prediction on the collection distribution, while a model deployed for planning or new goals may need predictions at states and actions rarely represented there. Broad counterfactual coverage and low on-distribution headroom are compatible. We propose examining the evaluation support before interpreting task success or a small context benefit as evidence about the need for explicit predictive structure. For learned policies or physical robots, this requires measurements under their own prediction and control conditions.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Dynamics randomization alone does not establish that a benchmark tests context inference. Our controlled examples show that similar predictive headroom can accompany very different kernel variation, and that observed state can retain evidence about hidden dynamics. Reporting this headroom would help distinguish limited opportunity for context inference from weaknesses of the methods being compared, making such benchmarks more informative about when explicit context inference in world models has information to add.

Independent Gaussian increments have per-coordinate variances σ 2 ​ Δ ​ t \sigma^{2}\Delta t for velocity and σ 2 ​ Δ ​ t 3 \sigma^{2}\Delta t^{3} for position, with σ = 0.1 \sigma=0.1 . A single reflection per axis at the workspace boundaries ± 2.5 \pm 2.5 reverses velocity with damping factor 0.5 0.5 . Initial position is uniform in [ − 0.5 , 0.5 ] 2 [-0.5,0.5]^{2} and initial velocity is zero. The sweep uses k ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 , 0.5 } k\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5\} . Before reflection, context changes only the Gaussian mean displacement, so the prior-weighted information is independent of the query. We evaluate both fixed and matched references from this interior kernel by one-dimensional quadrature for each coordinate. For visited scores, we compute the reflected density by summing its preimages with their Jacobians. Attractor posterior fitting. Five episode-level folds produce nearest-neighbor class frequencies from standardized position and velocity, with one Laplace pseudo-count for each of the four contexts. Actions are independent uniform draws, so the posterior uses state features only. Neighbor counts in { 128,256,512 , 1024 } \{128,256,512,1024\} are compared by context log loss on the same scored folds. At each logged next state, the estimator subtracts the fitted mixture log density from the true-context log density and averages over all transitions. The 1000 1000 percentile bootstrap resamples use fixed episode sums and counts, without refitting or repeating neighbor selection. These intervals summarize sampling variation conditional on the fitted predictions, not the full estimation uncertainty. Even known component kernels do not make the visitation-dependent posterior exact. As a local check, immediately after a zero-velocity position reset the context posterior is the known uniform prior. At reset interval ten, the fitted mean log-density contrast on those transitions is 1.0110 1.0110 nats, versus 0.9961 0.9961 when using the known prior. At interval two the corresponding values are 1.0093 1.0093 and 1.0071 1.0071 . This checks the estimator on the reset stratum, not on all visited states.

Estimation. MiniGrid’s structural reference is uniform over interior positions, four directions, and seven actions. There, we enumerate the kernels and integrate the continuous context prior. Visited headroom averages exact kernel KL divergences against mixtures fitted at each ( s , a ) (s,a) pair, leaving out the scored episode and applying one pseudo-count of smoothing. In Attractor, we use its query-invariant interior Gaussian kernel for the prior references. Its visited estimate scores logged next states under the known kernels, including boundary reflection, against a mixture with a five-fold, episode-split nearest-neighbor context posterior. The reset comparisons show that context information accumulates in state, including velocity, but do not isolate its effect from changes in coverage. 4 Implications for evaluating world models Low headroom can explain a small gain from explicit context inference when the observed state already supplies most of the evidence needed for prediction. High headroom instead indicates that revealing context can improve prediction. However, one should separately measure which information a learned representation retains and how well its predictor uses it, since a context encoder can still improve learning or approximation even when headroom is low. Comparisons of predictors with and without explicit context inference should therefore measure both the information available in the inputs and the errors of the actual models under matched data and compute. We propose reporting whether a benchmark’s context-conditional kernels remain predictively distinct at overlapping observed states. This requires specifying the collection rule, predictive inputs, transition weighting, and marginal context frequencies d ⁡ ( θ ) d(\theta) relative to the design prior. A low matched reference suggests changing the queries or perturbations, whereas a large matched-to-visited reduction requires distinguishing context imbalance from information retained in state. Increasing the parameter range alone does not resolve either issue reliably. We can compute these comparisons from context labels and simulator kernels, but with learned kernels we must also account for prediction error. Initial-state distributions, episode length, and observed physical coordinates also influence how much context remains hidden. A reset that changes position but preserves velocity can retain context information that the benchmark is intended to withhold. We therefore recommend reporting matched-query variation under each reset protocol’s collection distribution to separate changes in the prediction support from changes in context weights when interpreting the resulting headroom. We note that our measurements concern one-step prediction on the collection distribution, while a model deployed for planning or new goals may need predictions at states and actions rarely represented there. Broad counterfactual coverage and low on-distribution headroom are compatible. We propose examining the evaluation support before interpreting task success or a small context benefit as evidence about the need for explicit predictive structure. For learned policies or physical robots, this requires measurements under their own prediction and control conditions. 5 Conclusion Dynamics randomization alone does not establish that a benchmark tests context inference. Our controlled examples show that similar predictive headroom can accompany very different kernel variation, and that observed state can retain evidence about hidden dynamics. Reporting this headroom would help distinguish limited opportunity for context inference from weaknesses of the methods being compared, making such benchmarks more informative about when explicit context inference in world models has information to add.
